b: CREATE TABLE makes a new table. You name each column and give it a data type.
Example: CREATE TABLE Student_info (Reg_No VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, First_name CHAR(25) NOT NULL, Surname CHAR(25) NOT NULL, Department INT NOT NULL);
CHAR(n) stores fixed-length text. VARCHAR(n) stores variable-length text up to n characters. INT stores whole numbers.

q.q: Which command creates a new table?
q.e: CREATE TABLE defines columns and types.

b: PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL.
NOT NULL means the column must always have a value. UNIQUE means no two rows can share the same value.
DEFAULT gives a value when none is supplied, for example DEFAULT 'Nigeria'.

q.q: Which constraint forces a value to always be present?

o: Uses Nigeria when no value is given
q.e: It fills in the value automatically.

b: A table can have only one primary key. Writing PRIMARY KEY on the column and again as PRIMARY KEY(Reg_No) at the end gives an error. Use one or the other.
Do not put a comma after the last column or constraint before the closing bracket.
Column names cannot contain a hyphen. Use underscores, and spell the name the same everywhere you use it.

q.q: How many primary keys can one table have?
q.e: A primary key can span several columns, but there is only one.
